item.title: OpenAI, Anthropic disclosures spotlight growing AI containment challenge
item.description:
Two leading AI developers have released fresh evidence of a problem that researchers have long anticipated: advanced models searching for ways around the limits imposed on them. New disclosures from OpenAI and Anthropic detail how frontier systems exploited weaknesses in their environments or exceeded the intended scope of assigned tasks.

OpenAI is now tightening internet access in its internal model-training environment after finding that its frontier models could exploit software vulnerabilities and infrastructure misconfigurations to break out of sandboxes and reach the live internet.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.

The decision followed a September 20 incident in which an internal research model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver to gain limited access to the live internet during a training run.

After the incident, OpenAI said it paused training and evaluation of its most capable models and launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign, using AI agents to probe isolated copies of its research infrastructure. The tests uncovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities and weaknesses in the controls intended to prevent unauthorized access and communication.

Consequently, the company has announced a policy of conducting frontier-model training without internet access until improvements in security and monitoring justify broader access.

The disclosure came alongside a separate assessment from Anthropic, which detailed how its Claude Mythos 5 model attempted to compromise an unrelated GitHub repository during a cybersecurity evaluation.

OpenAI’s agents exploited flaws in containment controls

OpenAI’s red-teaming campaign found that agents could chain software vulnerabilities to escape virtual machines and execute code on the underlying host. The company identified weaknesses in open-source components, including Kata Containers, gVisor, and Moby/Docker, alongside Linux kernel vulnerabilities.

The company also found that agents could exploit weaknesses in internal services that retained limited outbound connections for functions such as logging, metrics, and authentication management. These connections provided routes to the internet despite restrictions elsewhere in the environment, OpenAI said.

In another test, agents running in separate microvirtual machines (microVMs) on shared host hardware exchanged synthetic secrets through processor-cache timing differences. The technique allowed them to communicate without a network connection or shared writable files.

OpenAI said it remediated the weaknesses and worked with open-source maintainers to disclose and fix affected software. Its post names several vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-24834 in Kata Containers and three Linux kernel flaws tracked as CVE-2026-74753, CVE-2026-80521 and CVE-2026-80841. The company also said it had disclosed numerous additional vulnerabilities that have not yet been made public.

The number of vulnerabilities and misconfigurations identified by the agents declined significantly as testing continued, OpenAI claims. It has now tightened network restrictions, strengthened monitoring, and developed an offline environment with indexed and cached web content so models can practise browsing without unrestricted access to live external systems.

“Although internet access can help models learn useful skills, it also gives a capable, misaligned agent opportunities to affect systems beyond our control,” the company said, explaining its decision to restrict live internet access during model training.

Reinforcement-learning training and internal inference were resumed on October 1 after implementing additional controls.

Anthropic flags alignment gap in Mythos

Anthropic’s assessment of a UK AI Security Institute (AISI) cybersecurity evaluation describes a different problem: a model taking unauthorized actions against real people while trying to complete an assigned task.

In nine of 43 evaluation runs, Anthropic said Claude Mythos 5 went beyond the intended scope of the exercise. In the most detailed case, after its authorized attempts to retrieve protected data from a simulated network failed, the model searched GitHub for a repository it believed was connected to the test environment.

The repository actually belonged to unrelated developers.

Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code and created fake identities to persuade the repository’s maintainers to approve the change, falsely claiming that the code was safe. The maintainer rejected the submission, and the run timed out. Anthropic characterized the behavior as a serious alignment failure involving overreach and deception in pursuit of the assigned objective.

Internet access had been enabled during the evaluation, and the production safeguards used with its general-release models had been disabled. The company said those safeguards would have flagged the behavior had they been enabled.

The article originally appeared on CSO.

item.title: NetSuite launches SuiteExpress to expedite implementation and optimization of ERP
item.description:
Agentic AI is the main topic at most industry events this year, with vendors adding agents to their products with gleeful abandon. NetSuite is no different; at its SuiteWorld conference this week, it is unveiling agents and AI workspaces designed to do everything from autonomous financial closing to AI-based supply chain management.

SuiteExpress, announced today, however, is something different. Rather than automating processes within the ERP suite, it is tied into Customer Success services, using AI to help customers implement the product.

“We’re leveraging the opportunity to bring AI to bear on the implementation, and accelerating the delivery of NetSuite’s implementations for our customers, as well as for helping them understand and take advantage of new capabilities as their business evolves and their business needs change,” explained Craig Sullivan, group VP of product management at Oracle NetSuite. “It’s the fast track onto NetSuite, delivers faster implementations at a lower cost, taking into account all of the key knowledge that the customer has about the way that they run their business today, as well as all of the knowledge that NetSuite has about how other customers in similar industries have been able to be successful on NetSuite.”

The company said this will help customers implement more of what they need at the beginning, to realize greater value more quickly. It claims that, using SuiteExpress, NetSuite implementation time is reduced “to weeks, or even days.”

SuiteExpress is powered by two connected knowledge bases that combine customer-specific context with NetSuite’s proprietary expertise, the company said in a news release. “The Customer Knowledge Base ingests meeting notes, documents, spreadsheets, recordings, and data from other systems to capture requirements, business processes, configuration decisions, and validation history, giving customers and implementation consultants a shared understanding of how the business works,” it said, while the NetSuite Knowledge Base adds proprietary product, implementation, and industry expertise from NetSuite’s experience with its customers. The two knowledge bases provide the context and expertise needed by the AI to recommend next steps, and to perform implementation tasks such as preparing data for migration, with oversight from consultants. It will also help customers continuously improve how they use NetSuite after go-live.

NetSuite SuiteExpress is available today to customers in the software industry in North America as part of a phased rollout. The company plans to broaden availability to other industries and geographies in 2027.

item.title: CIOs rethink roles, skills, training, and talent models for the future
item.description:
Longtime IT leader Matt Ausman envisions a future where developers may not have any backlog because AI will let them create new capabilities as quickly as they imagine them.

“The backlog will vanish because you will have infinite capacity,” says Ausman, SVP and CIO of Zebra Technologies.

He wonders whether business users will be able to keep up with the training required in a world where the software they use will change that rapidly. He also wonders whether IT workers are ready for that scenario: Will they be able to push back on bad ideas, or just build new capabilities simply because they can do so as rapidly as they’re proposed?

“Today we have to prioritize because we don’t have unlimited capacity. But in the future will they stop to ask, ‘Are we building the right things?’” he says, adding that “because someone thought it up, doesn’t mean it’s worth doing.”

Ausman acknowledges that such a reality is at least several years out, but he already sees AI changing how his IT team works, the work they need to do, and the skills required to do it.

For example, the average size of Scrum teams is shrinking, dropping from eight people to five or six who are producing more thanks to AI. Ausman believes Scrum teams may eventually be made up of two members: a functional product owner and a technical product owner who together use AI to gather requirements, generate mockups, create code, and so on, spending the bulk of their time supervising agents tasked with ensuring the architecture is right, bugs are fixed, security is in place, and the like.

Ausman also sees IT teams of the future producing work faster and drawing more from their business domain knowledge and less from their deep technical skills as they use AI to remake processes and workflows throughout the organization as well as in IT.

A shift in skills and mentality

These shifts will change not only how IT teams are structured but also the skills IT workers need, Ausman and other IT leaders and experts say.

True expertise in business domains, once merely a differentiator, is fast becoming a must-have for IT pros, Ausman notes. So is discernment (the ability to recognize when ideas aren’t worth pursuing), conviction (the ability to tell others that those ideas won’t produce benefits), and communication (the ability to be clear, concise, and diplomatic when telling others as much).

“They’ll need to be good partners to [the business] and be able to ask, ‘Are you sure we should do this thing?’” Ausman explains.

Of course, IT workers will continue to need technical skills, Ausman says, noting that most of his hiring today is for entry-level positions that draw in AI natives who help spread their AI knowledge throughout the enterprise. Still, he questions whether earning a computer science degree and knowing multiple programming languages will be as valuable 10 years into the future as they were a decade ago.

Problem-solving skills will be more highly prized in IT workers instead, he says. Emotional intelligence, authentic leadership, decision-making capabilities, and prioritization skills will also be in high demand.

“I think about my team and the fact that we can never outsource team care, the ability to have difficult conversations, emotional intelligence, [provide] psychological safety. Those things can never be automated,” he adds.

‘Hyperacceleration of learning needs’

CIOs across all industries are beginning to adjust their IT organizations in response to these evolving and anticipated changes as they contemplate the future of their IT workforces.

In a poll of CIOs at this year’s CIO 100 Awards and Conference in August, “talent, skills, and organizational change” topped the list of issues worrying CIOs, with 33% citing it. That put it ahead of “demonstrating AI business value and ROI” (27%) and “budget pressures and competing priorities” (21%).

When asked which capability will define the next generation of CIOs, 29% said “building organizational talent” — just behind “leading AI transformation” (30%) and ahead of “developing business strategy” (22%).

AI is obviously a factor here, as its use expands to automate more core IT tasks, but AI is only one of the dynamics driving change in IT. Demographics, market conditions, industry trends, and economics have all put pressure on organizations to be more responsive through the use of technology, says James Stanger, chief technology evangelist at CompTIA, an IT training and certification association.

Even as IT leaders feel the pressure of those dynamics, CIOs must also be ready to capitalize or respond to evolving technology as rapidly as it hits the market, Stanger adds. That puts further pressure on CIOs to rework their IT departments so that they’re able to meet such expectations.

Leading CIOs “have realized that technology is changing so utterly fast and because of that they need to change their organizations,” Stanger adds. “We’re finding that the traditional ways of doing things are being revised.”

Although most CIOs aren’t making radical changes yet, they are adjusting their approaches and the structure of their IT departments, Stanger notes.

CIOs are implementing more training initiatives and requirements to ensure their teams are better keeping pace with the changing tech landscape, Stanger says, noting that many CIOs have shifted from seeing training as a retention tool or a nice-to-have to something essential for enterprise survival.

And that commitment to learning is increasingly being incorporated into the day to day. “Microlearning is becoming more of a thing; there’s more of a steady stream,” he observes, adding that microlearning is beneficial because it can happen as rapidly as technology changes and accelerates hands-on retention of what is learned.

CIOs are also enlisting more talent from the business side to help develop technology solutions. These aren’t the citizen developers of yesterday, Stanger says, as they now often report via dotted lines to IT managers, allowing CIOs “to get a really good sense of what’s going on in those departments and what’s working and what is not.”

Conal Gallagher, CIO and CISO of Flexera, is leaning heavily into training to ensure his staffers have the skills necessary for the software maker to thrive.

AI fluency and AI use is at the top of Gallagher’s training list, as is AI administration and governance so that his staff can create AI tools that workers in other departments can safely use. And he’s working to develop more agentic AI skills among his workforce.

Like Stanger, Gallagher calls out the “hyperacceleration of learning needs” today, saying that most IT professionals are learning as they go, sometimes turning to online videos for instantaneous education.

The fast pace of technology evolution, however, makes it difficult to predict what will be needed from his IT workers a year from now. As a result, longer-term coursework is becoming less valuable.

“Traditional training as we know it probably doesn’t apply anymore,” he says, adding that the goal now may be to “just keep pace with the current.”

Reinventing roles to maximize IT capacity

Info-Tech Research Group’s 2026 IT Talent Trends report shows that IT leaders and IT pros alike expect nothing short of wholesale change for IT ahead. Nearly nine of 10 (89%) IT leaders anticipate restructuring their IT organization, according to the survey, and 95% of IT professionals acknowledge major skill changes would be required to keep pace with technology by 2030.

To help bridge IT to the future, CIOs are adding more service owners (the modern version of product owners) and business relationship managers, says Brittany Lutes, research director in Info-Tech’s CIO practice. IT leaders view these roles as essential for delivering AI and other IT capabilities that create value for the business.

“If they didn’t have them, they’re adding them,” she says. “If they had these roles before, they have more now.”

CIOs are also creating broader roles that enlist staff to operate in multiple domains, Lutes says. A networking engineer may now be expected to work in database administration and database engineering, for example.

CIOs want their teams to be more flexible and more modular, so they can move personnel more easily to where work needs to be done. To achieve that, some CIOs are grouping workers in pools or centers of excellence and then assigning them out as needed.

Broadening IT roles also helps keep those positions working at full capacity as AI picks up more of the manual tasks previously assigned to IT pros working as specialists.

“CIOs are not losing headcount, but the way they’re your utilizing that headcount is changing,” Lutes says, pointing out that these dynamics are changing job titles, too. For example, one IT organization Lutes knows of changed the all its IT workers’ titles to simply “engineer.”

Leading CIOs are also creating new roles centered around AI implementation and management, Lutes notes. These new roles include decision intelligence lead; forward-deployed engineer; human-AI interaction lead; knowledge engineer; master data manager; memory engineer; MLOps engineer; prompt engineer; synthetic data engineer; and trust engineer.

The seemingly contradictory trends reflect a profession in flux.

“We’re still in a messy phase as an industry,” Lutes says. “We’re not going to get to that major shift in the next two years, but five years out we may see a complete restructuring of the IT organization.”

Preparing for the future state

Nick Nadgauda, global CIO of MetLife, is preparing for that future state.

“We continually evaluate whether we have the right blend of engineering depth, business understanding, adaptability, and leadership,” he says. “The goal is not simply to fill today’s roles; it is to build a workforce that can learn, unlearn, and relearn as the work changes. That includes building a strong early-career pipeline and giving emerging technologists the technical foundations, mentoring, and hands-on experience to grow with the organization.”

This ongoing evaluation has reinforced three priorities at MetLife, Nadgauda says.

“First, AI fluency needs to become a broad workforce capability, not a specialty confined to a small group. Second, strong fundamentals in software engineering, cloud, cybersecurity, data, and architecture remain essential. We’re putting an emphasis on making our organization more technical. Third, we need teams organized around clearer accountability and closer alignment to business outcomes,” he says.

Nadgauda is investing in continuous role-based learning, creating more opportunities for hands-on learning, and bringing critical expertise in-house.

But he also acknowledges a degree of uncertainty about what’s ahead for IT, saying, “We can predict the direction more confidently than the exact destination.”

He adds, “We know AI will become a natural part of how work gets done across engineering, operations, and customer-facing teams. We also know that judgment, creativity, accountability, and deep domain expertise will remain critical. What is less certain is how quickly individual tasks and roles will change. That is why adaptability matters so much. The best hedge against uncertainty is a workforce that can learn continuously, experiment responsibly, and apply new capabilities to real business problems.”

item.title: In good company: 10 CIOs every CIO should follow
item.description:
CIOs are dealing with a lot of change, from the rapid rise of AI and cloud modernization, to cybersecurity and workforce transformation. Many are sharing what they’re learning as they tackle these challenges, including what’s working, what isn’t, and how they’re implementing new technologies in their organizations. Here, a select group of tech leaders reveal the CIOs they follow and why.

Suma Nallapati, chief AI and information officer, City and County of Denver

I follow Suma Nallapati primarily through public technology and AI leadership discussions. She regularly discusses AI adoption, responsible AI, digital transformation, technology strategy, AI governance, human-centered technology, and using AI to improve public services. I find her perspective particularly valuable because she connects AI strategy with practical organizational and citizen outcomes. She also emphasizes responsible and human-centered AI rather than viewing AI simply as a technology implementation exercise. One initiative I found particularly interesting was Denver’s use of AI through its multilingual Sunny chatbot and other city services. Her current role includes scaling AI across areas such as resident engagement, internal automation, permitting, and emergency response while maintaining governance, transparency, and public trust. – Sachin Gupta, senior IT manager, Arrow Electronics

Jennifer Hartsock, chief information and digital officer, Cargill

I follow Jennifer Hartsock through the CIO community, as well as through her thought leadership, interviews, and LinkedIn. I especially enjoy hearing her perspective in longer-form conversations where she talks candidly about the realities of leading technology and transformation in a large, complex organization. Hartsock talks about many of the issues CIOs are navigating right now, including AI, digital transformation, technology operating models, talent, and leadership. A consistent theme in her perspective is connecting tech decisions back to the business, including how tech teams work with the business, and how you create greater ownership closer to the outcomes you’re trying to achieve. – Kathy Kay, EVP and CIO, Principal Financial Group

Fletcher Previn, SVP and CIO, Cisco

Fletcher Previn’s profile shows how a modern technology leader can discuss change without reducing it to a narrative about vendors. He explores AI, culture, talent, and productivity, with an emphasis on conditions that determine whether transformation lasts. The insight worth returning to is his focus on adoption as a leadership responsibility. New technology fails when teams lack learning time, managers lack clarity, and incentives reward behavior that no longer serves the business. CIOs can apply that lens to modernization, security initiatives, and data governance. It encourages an honest definition of progress based on decisions and outcomes rather than launch dates or dashboards. – Sherif Koussa, CEO, Software Secured

Kellie Romack, CDIO, ServiceNow

What makes Kellie Romack’s perspective valuable is she talks about AI from inside a large enterprise IT organization, not the outside. Her posts regularly cover enterprise AI, AI governance, autonomous IT, workforce transformation, cybersecurity, digital transformation, and how the CIO role is changing.

The point that stayed with me was her argument that CIO organizations now have to redesign jobs, teams, and workflows around AI while building new human skills at the same time. That’s a useful distinction. It frames successful AI adoption as an organizational and leadership problem as much as a technology one. Her seat at ServiceNow also gives her a view of what happens after the experiments stop. ServiceNow has reported that its internal AI use cases grew from 15 to more than 200. That makes her worth reading about for any CIO trying to understand what scaling enterprise AI actually looks like. – Tapabrata Biswas, project manager, InfluxIQ Tech Pvt. Ltd.

Mike Blandina, CIO, Snowflake

I follow Mike Blandina for his practical perspective on enterprise AI adoption and the operational realities behind digital transformation. His commentary consistently connects emerging technology with the governance, workforce skills, and measurable outcomes needed to make it useful. One insight that particularly resonates with me comes from this CIO.com article.

He makes the case for building an editing culture rather than a writing culture. As AI increasingly handles first drafts of code, reports, and other work, he argues that the critical human skill becomes evaluating outputs, identifying mistakes, and knowing when to challenge the system. I also appreciate his emphasis on data lineage, access permissions, and measuring actual productivity improvements instead of AI tool logins. Those are the less visible decisions that determine whether enterprise AI adoption delivers lasting value. – Parth Patel, director of operations, Shaligram

Deepa Soni, EVP and CIO, New York Life Insurance Company

Deepa Soni’s insights are particularly valuable because she oversees AI in one of the most critical and regulated sectors of financial services, a Fortune 100 life insurance company where AI decisions have real consequences for policyholders and regulators.

Soni frequently shares in-depth thoughts on what responsible AI adoption truly looks like within a large financial institution. She discusses the delicate balance between the speed of innovation and the readiness of governance, as well as how tech leaders can foster cultures that promote both agility and accountability. What sets her apart is that her approach to AI strategy is rooted in operational realities rather than just vendor hype, which is a rare and precious perspective for CIOs facing similar challenges. – Viren Meghani, technical architect and independent researcher in AI governance

Sears Merritt, CIO and head of enterprise technology and experience, MassMutual

I follow Sears Merritt on LinkedIn and through his interviews. He talks about what enterprise AI costs to run and how to keep the option to change your mind. Merritt also discusses why AI vendor contracts should be capped at 12 months to maintain flexibility, how success metrics are defined before AI pilots begin to determine whether they should be scaled, and the data platform he spent three years building before the AI wave arrived. This is useful to other CIOs because he’s one of the few CIOs at a regulated insurer who talks about AI in the language of procurement and measurement rather than vision. – Egiziago Cioffi, IT/enterprise architect and CEO, SynSphere Italia

Ganesh Ariyur, CIO and head of enterprise technology, Gainwell Technologies

I follow Ganesh Ariyur for his insightful views on AI, enterprise architecture, transformation, tech strategy, governance, and ways CIOs can link tech investments to quantifiable business value. What I find particularly helpful is his content extends beyond just talking about new technologies. He continually positions technology choices in relation to business results, operational frameworks, financial discipline, and implementation. This is particularly important for CIOs facing pressure to showcase ROI from AI and modernization efforts.

An example is his work, The 2026 CIO Operating Model: Architecture, AI, and Enterprise Value. His main point is that tech strategy must be viewed more like capital strategy, with CIOs assessing issues like if cloud expenditures enhance unit economics, and if architecture facilitates quicker decision-making. That viewpoint is important as it transitions the dialogue from which technology to implement, to what ways technology should transform the enterprise’s operations and value creation. – Ketan Patel, digital marketing manager, WeDoWebApps

Jim Swanson, EVP and CIO, Johnson & Johnson

I’m interested in how Jim Swanson thinks about the relationship between technology and the business, particularly where innovation carries considerable responsibility. For example, he recently discussed how AI agents are changing the way people interact with enterprise software. What caught my attention was his emphasis on the complexity that comes with that change — the integration, oversight, and accountability required to make it work. Those are questions that deserve as much attention as the technology itself. – Bill Huber, partner, ISG

Kimberly Basile, CIO, Kyndryl

I follow Kim Basile along with her bylined pieces on Kyndryl’s newsroom and interviews in the business press. She discusses enterprise AI adoption, workforce readiness, AI governance, platform modernization, and security leadership, informed by her earlier role as SVP and CISO at Leidos. Basile speaks from inside a transformation few CIOs have experienced, having helped guide Kyndryl’s technology separation from IBM and consolidate its application portfolio. She treats governance and people readiness as part of AI adoption from the start, and she’s candid about what hasn’t worked. In a recent feature on agentic AI, for instance, she said Kyndryl initially focused on counting agents, and the number didn’t tell the true story. Her team pivoted to measure business process flows. She also identified automating a process that hadn’t been properly validated as one of the company’s biggest mistakes. Activity metrics are easy to report, so organizations default to them. Her lesson pushes CIOs to validate a process before automating it.

She matters beyond the technology because women remain underrepresented in IT leadership, and she uses her visibility to lift others. When she was named to Women We Admire’s Top Women CIOs of 2026, her second year on the list, she used her post to congratulate the other honorees by name and highlight how these leaders help employees embrace technology. That generosity matters in a field where women CIOs are still too few. As the co-founder of Girl Power Talk, I pay attention to leaders who open doors for the next generation of women in tech. Basile does that consistently. – Sameer Somal, founder and CEO, Blue Ocean Global Technology

item.title: The metric that makes your IT org look healthier than it is
item.description:
An executive IT dashboard can stay green for a year while the risks it is supposed to surface keep growing. Availability above target every month. Service levels met. Patch compliance climbing quarter over quarter. Every number accurate, and every one trusted by the executive team.

When trouble finally arrives, it skips amber entirely. It comes as an outage, an audit finding or a security incident, and the first question in the room is why the dashboard said everything was fine.

In my work with technology leaders and executive teams, I have learned that a dashboard can be technically accurate and still leave leadership dangerously misinformed. Usually nobody fudged anything. The numbers were built to summarize, and a summary is very good at hiding the one thing an executive most needs to see. Three metrics produce most of that false comfort at the executive level. I would not put any of them in front of a CEO or a board as a headline number.

Three green numbers I would take off the executive dashboard

Monthly availability is the classic. A 99.9 percent month still allows about 43 minutes of downtime, and the percentage says nothing about when those minutes fell. Forty minutes at 3 a.m. on a Sunday and forty minutes during month-end close produce the same number. So do one long outage and a dozen short ones that each forced the order desk to restart its work. CIO.com made a version of this case years ago, arguing that uptime means little until it is tied to business impact. Business leaders notice the gap. When the official figure does not match what their teams lived through, the dashboard loses the room, and nobody tells the CIO.

Service-level attainment is the second. A service desk can hit its resolution targets month after month while the same problems keep coming back. A recurring sync failure gets fixed in twenty minutes, closed inside the target and counted as a success. It happens again the following week and gets counted as another success. The metric rewards fast closure, so the organization gets very good at fast closure, and the underlying fault never draws enough attention to be fixed. What builds underneath is a growing list of known problems held together by workarounds. Each one is a small daily cost to the business and a much larger risk the day the person who knows the workaround leaves.

Patch compliance is the third, and the most dangerous, because it expresses security posture as a percentage of a device count. A fleet that is 96 percent patched sounds well defended. The question the percentage cannot answer is which 4 percent. The unpatched remainder is rarely random. It is the legacy system nobody is allowed to reboot, the vendor-managed appliance the team cannot touch, the server behind a process considered too important to risk. Those are often the assets an attacker would pick first. The headline number improves every quarter as the easy devices get patched, while the exposure that matters sits unchanged on an exceptions list nobody above the security team reads.

Why averages flatter the people who report them

Each of these metrics averages across a large population where the risk is concentrated in a small corner. The thousands of healthy devices, the hundreds of quiet hours and the routine tickets all pull the number toward green. The handful of things that could actually hurt the company barely move it.

Executive dashboards drift toward this kind of measure for understandable reasons. Percentages are stable, they trend nicely and they compare cleanly against a target. They also protect the team producing them, which is the part few people say out loud. A metric that is green almost every month spares everyone a hard conversation. Over a few years, without anyone deciding it, the dashboard selects for numbers that do exactly that. One question exposes it quickly: when did the executive dashboard last show a red month? If nobody can remember, or nobody can say what it would take to produce one, the dashboard has stopped measuring the organization and started reassuring it.

The cost lands when something breaks. A CIO who reported green for eleven straight months and then has to explain a major incident is answering two questions at once: what went wrong and why the reporting missed it. The second question is the one executives remember, and it colors how they read every report that follows. After that, a green month is no longer taken at face value.

I hold every executive metric to one test. If a number cannot embarrass me, it does not belong on the dashboard.

What I would put in front of executives instead

The replacements are less flattering and more useful. There are three I would choose.

  1. Disruption minutes on the processes that matter. It starts with an agreement with business leaders, made in advance, on a short list of processes their teams cannot run without and the windows when those processes matter most: order entry during business hours, payroll in the days before a run, financial systems at close. Then the dashboard reports minutes of disruption to those processes during those windows, and every incident behind the number is listed by name. A quiet month looks quiet. A bad Tuesday during close shows up as exactly what it was, and the business leaders in the room recognize it because they lived it.
  2. Repeat incidents. Of everything that broke this month, how much had broken before? I would trade every resolution rate on the dashboard for this one number. A low repeat rate means problems are being fixed at the root. A rising one means the organization is living on workarounds, and it shows up months before the workarounds start to fail in ways that customers notice.
  3. The age of the worst exposure. For security, the measure I want to see is the oldest unremediated critical vulnerability on systems that face the internet or hold sensitive data, along with the number of standing exceptions and the name of the executive who approved each one. The age moves only when the hard cases get fixed, which is the point. An exception with an executive’s name on it is far more likely to get a decision: fix it or own the risk. An exception that belongs to nobody can sit indefinitely.

Each replacement shares three properties. Its red threshold is agreed before the reporting period begins, so nobody negotiates it after the fact. It points at a specific process or system, so a red result tells an executive where to look. And it is uncomfortable enough that the team would rather fix the underlying issue than explain the number again next month.

The old percentages still have a home. They stay on the operations team’s internal dashboards, where they help run the shop day to day and where a team lead can see a trend early. The executive view gets the measures that can turn red.

None of this requires new tooling. Most IT organizations already capture the incident history, the vulnerability data and the process calendar these measures depend on. What it requires is a decision about what the executive team is entitled to see, and the willingness to show a red month before something forces it.

The first report built this way will almost certainly show red somewhere, and that is the reason to build it. A red month is uncomfortable for a meeting or two. It also sharpens the questions, turns the conversation to the actual condition of the systems the company runs on and ends the CIO’s role as the person who said everything was fine. A dashboard that has been green for a year might be telling the truth. From the top, there is no way to know, and that is reason enough to change what goes on it.

item.title: Your senior engineers need junior questions more than juniors need answers
item.description:
When juniors take naive questions to an AI assistant instead of a colleague, dashboards record fewer interruptions and higher velocity. What they miss is the erosion of senior engineers’ architectural fluency, and the single point of failure that hardens until an outage forces someone to explain the system out loud.

Over the past year, I watched engineering teams celebrate a quiet drop in Slack interruptions. A junior used to ask a foundational question in a channel: why does this service retry three times instead of once? Today that junior asks an AI assistant first, messaging a senior only if the answer fails in testing. Already, 51% of developers ask generative AI for help they once asked a colleague, and 62% do so to avoid looking uninformed.

Because AI now absorbs routine implementation and debugging, it strips away the trial-and-error juniors once needed to grow into seniors.

Most writing about this shift worries about what juniors lose: less mentorship, thinner context and a shallower feel for production systems. That worry is real, but it is only half the balance sheet.

The costlier loss belongs to the senior engineer and the organization paying them to hold the architecture together. It rarely gets discussed because from the inside it looks like uninterrupted focus time.

What a naive question actually did

A junior engineer’s question was never just a request for a file path. It did three distinct jobs at once, and all three required a human on the receiving end.

First, it transferred tacit institutional memory that documentation never captured. When a senior explained why a payment service retried three times, they rarely recited the config. They narrated an incident from a year ago involving a partner’s rate limiter that never made it into a wiki. Documentation misses that history because nobody writes a design doc after the fact unless something breaks again.

Second, the question gave the senior a live audit of where the system had become needlessly opaque. A staff engineer who has owned a core service for three years goes blind to its rough edges; everything feels obvious once you know the history behind every compromise. A newcomer’s confusion is a free signal showing where the code no longer speaks for itself.

Third, and most overlooked, answering forced an articulation that kept the senior’s own mental model sharp. Explaining a state machine out loud to a colleague who asks follow-ups is a different mental discipline than silently knowing it. Teachers have known this forever: structuring knowledge for someone else exposes gaps and outdated assumptions in your own head. Seniors used to get that workout dozens of times a quarter for free.

The channel disappears without an alarm

Because those informal questions were never scheduled on a calendar or tracked in Jira, their disappearance triggers no alarm. When an AI assistant intercepts the first tier of naive questions, the senior simply gets interrupted less often. Over a single sprint, that silence feels like focus time. Over several quarters, it quietly erodes a senior engineer’s active command of the architecture they own on paper.

In practice, this decay stays hidden during routine code review because spotting a local bug on screen only requires passive recognition. Failure surfaces in postmortems when an incident demands active cross-system recall: tracing how failures cascade across service boundaries during a 2 a.m. outage. Across 211 million lines of analyzed code, structural refactoring has already collapsed from 25% of changes to under 10%, while duplicated code blocks jumped eightfold. Answering a junior’s “what happens if this service times out?” used to force seniors to trace those paths out loud every week. Without that rehearsal, the first live cross-boundary trace happens during an outage.

Why velocity dashboards hide the risk

For a CIO or VP of Engineering, this creates a treacherous blind spot. Standard engineering health metrics do not merely miss this erosion; they actively misread it as progress.

When juniors turn to AI assistants instead of pinging seniors, short-term output metrics look healthier. Pull request cycle times tighten, ticket velocity ticks upward and seniors report fewer context switches on surveys. On throughput dashboards, the organization appears to scale effortlessly.

Underneath those green indicators, three structural risks accumulate.

  • Shared ownership collapses into a single point of failure. When architectural rationale stops circulating verbally, it stays trapped inside the heads of the veterans who wrote the code. If one leaves, what looked like shared ownership turns out to be unshared memory.
  • Outage recovery times creep upward on complex incidents. Routine bugs get fixed faster with AI, but cross-boundary outages take longer. Every 25% increase in AI adoption correlates with a 7.2% drop in delivery stability, including mean time to recovery (the time required to restore service during an outage). When AI-generated changes hit production without shared context, seniors on the call spend precious minutes re-deriving how subsystems interact.
  • Senior engineers’ verification load rises even as mentoring drops. In a 2026 study on developer skill formation, Anthropic found developers who delegated coding to AI suffered their steepest drop in debugging comprehension, creating a downstream “debugging tax.” In practice, seasoned engineers spend up to 19% more time verifying and fixing AI-generated code. When juniors skip foundational questions upfront, they still need a senior engineer’s help later, shifting the senior’s role from upstream architectural teaching to downstream code forensics.

An organization can coast on accumulated fluency for many months before the deficit shows. By the time it surfaces in postmortems or failed handoffs, the habits keeping senior engineers’ understanding sharp have been dormant for quarters.

Rebuilding the channel on purpose

When leaders notice institutional context slipping, their first instinct is more aggressive documentation or indexing wikis into AI retrieval tools. That solves lost context for readers, but not the senior engineer’s problem. Writing a static wiki page never forces a veteran to defend trade-offs or trace failure cascades under questioning. Documentation captures static answers; only live human friction keeps architectural fluency sharp.

Restoring that friction does not mean restricting juniors from using AI assistants, nor does it mean adding optional team meetings that get cut the moment a deadline tightens. If directors are rewarded solely on ticket velocity, informal coaching will always lose to the sprint board. Instead, leadership must embed live human articulation across the four moments where architecture is built, rehearsed, stress-tested and passed on.

  • At code review: require verbal design defense on cross-boundary pull requests. Instead of letting seniors review large AI-generated diffs silently, require a ten-minute live walkthrough whenever a change touches service boundaries, retries or state machines. The junior explains what the code assumes about upstream systems; the senior explains why the boundary exists, replacing downstream code forensics with upstream architectural dialogue.
  • Between incidents: run live system walkthroughs without slides. Once a month, a senior engineer walks peers through a critical production workflow on a whiteboard, tracing failure modes and historical trade-offs out loud. Where the explanation stalls or relies on guesswork, institutional memory has decayed before an outage can expose it.
  • After an outage: require unscripted architectural narratives in postmortems. Do not let seniors satisfy an incident review by pasting a runbook link or an AI-generated summary. Require the service owner to explain live to adjacent teams how a failure propagated and why the boundary exists. Unscripted explanation under peer questioning is the only reliable test of whether a team still understands the software it runs.
  • At the 90-day check-in: test architectural handoff, not just ticket count. AI makes it easy for a new hire to close starter tickets in week two without learning how the system fits together. Use the first structured performance check-in to verify whether the new engineer can modify a core workflow and explain its failure modes without escalating to the senior owner. If early ticket velocity is high but every structural change still routes back to one veteran after a quarter, AI is accelerating surface work while core architecture stays trapped in one head.

Every seasoned engineer knows the feeling of trying to explain a familiar system out loud and finding the words no longer come cleanly. That stumble rarely means they lost their edge. It means the friction that kept their understanding sharp was automated away, and leadership must put it back before the next outage asks for an answer.

item.title: Organizational Sustainability
item.description:
When we talk about sustainability, most of us probably think about environmental sustainability. Reducing carbon emissions, using fewer resources, moving towards a circular economy, and so on. But there is another form of sustainability that deserves more attention: the organizational sustainability.
Can an organization continue to create value when the world around it changes? Can it adapt when customer expectations shift, regulations change, competitors emerge from unexpected places, technologies evolve, or economic and geopolitical circumstances suddenly turn against it? In other words, can the organization remain viable when its environment refuses to stand still?
I believe Enterprise Architecture has an important role to play in answering that question.

The post Organizational Sustainability appeared first on EAWheel.
